Text S1. Properties and characterization of Fe-C particles used in this study

Fe-C particles (Fig. S1a) with a specific surface area of 1.2 m2/g, physical strength of 800 kg/m2, bulk density of 1100~1300 g/L, and porosity greater than 65 % (this data is from the supplier), were prepared by washing with diluted H2SO4 solution and deionized water to scour off the oxide coating on the surface (Huang et al., 2022).

Analysis via scanning electron microscope (SEM) illustrates the rough, porous surface structure of Fe-C particles possessing adsorption properties (Fig. S1b). Numerous small iron particles adhered to the surface of Fe-C particles and penetrated the particles' interior through embedding or encapsulation. EDS (Fig. S1c) and XPS (Fig. S1d) analyses indicate that the elements in the Fe-C particles are mainly dominated by C, O, Fe, and Si. The XRD spectra (Fig. S1e) show that the iron in the Fe-C particles is mainly dominated by Fe0 and Fe3O4. Additionally, the iron content in the Fe-C particles was verified to exceed 50% via testing conducted using an ICP-OES instrument (Agilent 5110 ICP-OES, America). The Fe-C particles exhibit a broad absorption peak at 3415 cm-1 (Fig. S1f), which is related to the stretching and bending vibrations of −OH, indicating that the surface contains a large number of −OH groups (Wang et al., 2013). The absorption peaks at 1630 cm-1 and 970 cm-1 correspond to the vibration of C=O and C-O, respectively (Lai et al., 2012). The infrared wavelength at 568 cm-1 is correlated with the stretching vibration of Fe-O in Fe3O4, while the absorption peak at 473 cm-1 is correlated with the vibration of γ-Fe2O3 (Ma et al., 2017).
Text S2. Microalgae cultivation in different treatment systems of biogas slurry

The biogas slurry from different treatment systems was filtered through a 0.45 μm filter membrane before being used for microalgae cultivation. The impact of varying pretreatment durations and dilutions of the biogas slurry on microalgae growth was confirmed through biomass changes assessed in a 96-well plate. Specifically, the biogas slurry underwent dilution at varying treatment durations—2, 5, and 10 times with deionized water—followed by microalgae inoculation after 1 day of nutrient deprivation. The prepared microalgae solution was dispensed into a 96-well plate and incubated in a constant-temperature light incubator (25°C) for 2 days. Biomass variations in microalgae (measured as OD680 values) were assessed pre-and post-incubation using an enzyme meter (Thermo Scientific Multiskan Sky, America).

The supernatant from RBS and treated biogas slurry was diluted 10-fold into 100 mL serum bottles and then inoculated with microalgae at 0.2 g/L. To regulate the nutrient ratios, 8.4 mg/L phosphate (TAP medium phosphate solution) was further supplemented to the biogas slurry. Regular sampling intervals were observed to analyze both the physiological characteristics of the microalgae and the utilization of pollutants in the biogas slurry. Microalgae were cultured in a lighted incubator at 25°C, cycling between 12-hour periods of cool-white fluorescent light at 5500 ± 100 lx and darkness. A 5% CO2 gas flow at 20 mL/min was maintained in the serum bottles throughout microalgae cultivation.
Text S3. Detailed test methods for water quality

Samples obtained in each system were filtered by a 0.45 μm membrane filter before the following measurements. Concentrations of NH4+-N, NO3--N, NO2--N, PO43--P, and TP were determined according to the Chinese State Environmental Protection Agency Standard Methods (SEPA, 2002). Turbidity is measured using a turbidimeter (Hash, 2100Q, America). Dissolved oxygen (DO) was measured using a portable dissolved oxygen meter (JPB-607A, Shanghai Leici, China). Total organic carbon (TOC) and total nitrogen (TN) were measured by a total organic carbon analyzer (TOC-VCPN, Shimadzu, Japan). UV−visible absorbance spectra were measured by UV spectroscope (M7, MAPADA, China). The concentration of Fe(II) and Fe(III) in the solution was determined by the phenanthroline spectrophotometry method at 512 nm (Tamura et al., 1974). Metal ion content was quantified using an inductively coupled plasma emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, Optima 2100DV, PerkinElmer, USA).

3D excitation−emission matrix (EEM) spectrofluorometry (Aqualog, Horiba, Japan) was used to characterize the fluorescent components. For this, a parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis was performed using the DOMFluor Toolbox in MATLAB 2023a software, as previously reported (Stedmon and Bro, 2008). The PARAFAC components were compared to previous studies by using the OpenFluor database (Murphy et al., 2014).
The EEM spectra were divided into five wavelength regions, and fluorescence regional integration (FRI) was calculated according to the following method (Chen et al., 2003).

The cumulative fluorescence intensity of DOM with similar properties can be obtained by integrating the integral volume (Φi) of a specific fluorescence region. Then Φi is normalized to obtain the integral standard volume (Φi,n) of a specific fluorescence region, thus reflecting the relative content of organic matter with specific structure in this region. Finally, the ratio of the integrated standard volume of a particular fluorescence region to the total integrated standard volume is calculated as Pi,n. The relevant formula is as follows:

Where Φi, Φi,n represent the integral volume and standard volume of fluorescence region i, respectively, au·nm2. λex and λem are the excitation and emission wavelengths, respectively, nm. MFi is the multiplication factor, i.e., the reciprocal of the ratio of the integrated area of a particular fluorescent region i to the total integrated area of the fluorescent region. I (λexλem) is the fluorescence intensity corresponding to the excitation and emission wavelengths, au. ΦT,n is the total fluorescence area-integrated standard volume, au·nm2. Pi,n is the ratio of the integrated standard volume of a particular fluorescence region i to the total integrated standard volume, %.
Text S5. 2D-COS analysis methods and details
For the spectral changes of y (n, t), as a function of a spectral variable (n) and an external variable (t), the dynamic spectrum (y(v,t)) is defined as follows:

Where y is the reference spectrum of the system, z(y2, t) is the Hilbert-transformed orthogonal spectrum, and Φ(v1,v2) and Ψ(v1,v2) are the 2D synchronous spectrum and 2D asynchronous spectrum, respectively.

The off-diagonal peaks in the synchronous graph represent the direction of characteristic signal change; the off-diagonal peaks on the asynchronous graph represent the sequence of signal responses. According to Noda’s rules, the judgment method is as follows: When both v1 and v2 are greater than or less than zero, v1 precedes v2; when one of v1 and v2 is positive, and the other is negative, v2 precedes v1.

The corresponding changes of different wavelengths can be obtained by analyzing the signal changes of UV spectra over time. In this study, functions were constructed to correlate the different treatment systems with time.
Text S6. Characterization of Fe-C corrosion products

The surface morphology of the Fe-C particles was observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS GeminiSEM 300, German), and the surface elemental composition and content were analyzed by electron spectroscopy (EDS). The characteristic crystal information of the Fe-C corrosion products was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Ultima IV, Japan).
Text S7. Electrode preparation methods and electrochemical testing

The Fe/C particles were dispersed in ethanol to prepare a suspension with a concentration of 10 mg/mL. A 5% Nafion solution was included as a binder and ultrasonically dispersed for 30 minutes. The fully dispersed Fe/C suspension was gradually added dropwise to the lower half (1 × 1 cm) of a 1 × 2 cm carbon paper multiple times. The upper half of the carbon paper was utilized to secure the electrode holder. The Fe/C loading on the working electrode was set at 1 mg. Electrochemical testing employed a 0.1 M NaCl solution. Pt and Ag/AgCl electrodes served as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Electrochemical testing was conducted concurrently with the reaction process.

Cyclic voltammetry (CV) analysis was conducted with a scanning voltage range of -1.0 V ~ +1.0 V and a scanning rate of 10 mV/s. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were carried out over a frequency range of 0.1 Hz ~ 1 MHz (Zhao et al., 2021). The EIS results were fitted using Zview 3.1 software (ZiffNet, USA).
Text S8. Determination of active species during the reaction

The presence of Fe (IV) was detected by the sulfoxide probe method. Methyl phenyl sulfoxide (PMSO) and methyl phenyl sulfone (PMSO2) concentrations were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 1260, USA) equipped with a UV detector and an Agilent Exend-C18 reversed-phase column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) (Liu et al., 2023). The amounts of •O2− and •OH are determined by nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) transformation and terephthalic acid photoluminescence (TA-PL) probing means, respectively (Huang et al., 2017).
Text S9. Elemental composition analysis of Fe-C particles and floc samples

The content of C, H, O, and N in the sample was tested by an organic element analyzer (Thermo Scientific Flash 2000, America). The metal element content of the samples was analyzed by ICP-OES instruments (Agilent 5110 ICP-OES, America).

Before the metal ion analysis, the sample underwent the following digestion process. The appropriate amount of sample was put into a polytetrafluoroethylene ablation tube and 1 mL of nitric acid (HNO3, 65%, SCR, China) and 1 mL of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 30%, SCR, China) were added to react for 12 h. After the reaction, 3 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl, 36%, SCR, China) was added. The samples were digested by an ablator at 60°C, 120°C, and 165°C for 1 h, 1 h, and 2 h, respectively. The liquid phase was evaporated through the residual temperature and then 0.5 mL of HNO3 was added. The samples were dissolved in deionized water and used for further analysis.

The surface functional groups of flocs were analyzed by Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR, Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS20, America). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha, America) was used to estimate the elemental composition and valence.
Text S10. SR-FTIR analysis of floc samples

The floc samples were dissolved in distilled water and dispersed by ultrasonication for 15 min. 150 μL of the suspension was dropped to the embedded bas and frozen at -20 °C. Thin sections (5 μm in thickness) were then cut on a cryosectioner (Leica CM1860, Germany). The samples were subsequently air-dried at room temperature so that the effect of the embedding agent on the infrared spectra of the samples could be neglected (Du et al., 2021). The Synchrotron radiation-based Fourier transform infrared (SR-FTIR) spectra were obtained at the beam-line BL01B1 of National Facility for Protein Science in Shanghai (NFPS). Spectra were recorded in reflectance mode using a Thermo Nicolet 6700 FT-IR spectrometer and a continuous infrared microscope to record regions of interest. Spectral maps were processed using the OPUS 8.1 software (Bruker Corporation, German).
Text S11. EXAFS test and analysis methods

Extended x-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) of coordination environment of Fe within flocs was analyzed by bulk Fe K-edge (7112 eV) on beamline BL14W1 of the NFPS. Data were acquired in transmission mode at room temperature. The pre-edge and post-edge information on samples and Fe foil were collected simultaneously to correct slight energy offsets. The obtained data was processed and analyzed using the Demeter software package (Ravel and Newville, 2005). Wavelet transform (WT) analysis of k3-weighted EXAFS spectra was implemented using MATLAB 2023a software (Funke et al., 2005). Linear combination fitting (LCF) was performed using k3-weighted EXAFS spectra in the range of k = 2-12.5 Å–1 for both experimental samples and reference minerals.
Text S12. Analysis of oxidative stress in microalgae cell

The microalgae suspension was centrifuged (8000 r, 2 min) to remove the medium and then washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) buffer 2~3 times. Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were quantified using dichlorodihydrofluorescein-diacetate (DCFH-DA) fluorescent dye (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China) (You et al., 2022). Microalgae cells resuspended in PBS were lysed using an ultrasonic homogenizer (Biosafer650-92, Nanjing Saifei Biotechnology Institute, China) at 500 W for 20 min at 3 s intervals. The supernatant obtained by centrifugation is the microalgal cell lysate. Appropriate amount of cell lysate was taken for measurement of CAT and MDA. CAT and MDA were determined using a CAT assay kit (Ultraviolet method) and an MDA assay kit (TBA method) (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China), respectively.
Text S13. Analysis of variation in TN, NH4+-N, and PO43--P

The variation in total nitrogen (TN) concentration is shown in Fig. S4d. All three systems exhibited a decreasing trend in the early stage which may be related to the adsorption of Fe-C particles and the blowing off of nitrogenous pollutants by microbubbles (Provolo et al., 2017). The TN concentration started to accumulate after 40 min, and reached 1485.50, 1394.25, and 1349.75 mg/L in the MFC, CFC, and MBs systems, respectively, after the operation. Almost all inorganic nitrogen in the biogas slurry is NH4+-N (Table S4b), which is difficult to remove by flocculation or oxidation. Therefore, the increase in dissolved organic nitrogen during the reaction was dominated by the increase in TN concentration.

Fe-C micro-electrolysis exhibited excellent removal capacities for phosphate from biogas slurry. Fig. 1c shows the variations in PO43--P and all PO43--P was removed (below the detection limit) from the MFC and CFC systems after operation. The removal efficiencies were 92.9% in the MFC system and 41.96% in the CFC system at the 10th minute, indicating that microbubbles increase the removal rate of PO43--P. The PO43--P in the water will form Fe3(PO4)2 and FePO4 precipitation with Fe(II) and Fe(III) dissolved from the Fe-C particles (Zheng et al., 2023). The precipitation and coagulation of Fe(OH)3 flocs in the water can also improve the effect of phosphorus removal (Huang et al., 2022). Moreover, based on the microbubbles assistance, Fe(II) will be further oxidized to Fe(III), and the situ generated Fe(III) will form a short-range ordered strengite-like structure (corner-linked PO4 tetrahedra to FeO6 octahedra) with phosphate to enhance phosphorus removal (Yang et al., 2023). The concentrations of phosphate decreased moderately with time in the MBs system. Some metal cations (e.g., Fe(II)/Fe(III), Ca(II), Al(III), Mg(II), etc.) in the biogas slurry were solubilized in the presence of acidic environment and microbubbles, which can form precipitates with phosphate, resulting in a decrease in phosphate concentration (He et al., 2022; Ogata et al., 2020).
Text S14. Analysis of UV 2D-COS results

UV 2D-COS was used to derive the removal mechanism of UV-active substances in different systems (Fig. S10). UV-synchronous correlation spectra of all systems exhibited intense auto peaks in the 200–240 nm range without any cross peaks. The drop in intensity sensitivity of the synchronized auto peak in the MFC system is higher than in the CFC system, illustrating that more UV-active substances are removed in the presence of microbubbles (Yu et al., 2022). Different cross-peaks were identified in the asynchronous spectra at 205, 230, 254, 270, and 290 nm. Previous studies demonstrated that 205 nm represents the absorption band of the benzenoid (Hur et al., 2011), while 254 and 270 nm correlate with electronic transitions in aromatic structures in humic-like substances (Yu et al., 2022). According to Noda’s rules (Noda, 1993), the asynchronous results showed the response sequence of the UV peak was 270>230>290>205>254 nm in the MFC system, 270>230>254 nm in the CFC system, and 205>290>254 nm in MBs system. This suggests that the reduction of benzenoid was more sensitive with microbubbles.
